\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where LP-quality alignment is strong, but gains are absent elsewhere despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We diagnose two causes: instance degeneracy (13\textendash 87\%) and weak LP-quality alignment; degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations).

Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes all three evaluated datasets.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Two factors shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples produce identical F1, (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) limits the available headroom; (b)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to MBR utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably predict instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.38 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82, CoNLL EM). \textbf{Right}: quality estimation does not translate to selection; all methods approximately match greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (AUPRC 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
    LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (\S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as the correct self-consistency analogy.}
    Rather than selecting one of $N$ outputs, aggregating entities across samples yields $+1.35$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.018$) and $+1.32$\,pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes all three evaluated datasets.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP gains are associated with strong LP-quality alignment (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two factors constrain selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) limits the available headroom, and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample) prevents exploiting the remainder.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 48.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation disentangles the two factors: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5--0.7; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Within fixed settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness: the SciERC epoch ablation shows LP gains varying with training-induced degeneracy (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}). Across 23 dataset-model-temperature configurations ($N{=}8$), however, degeneracy alone does not predict LP direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$); LP signal quality and dataset characteristics are required for cross-dataset prediction.
Temperature and training convergence are controllable levers for degeneracy (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 86.5\% vs.\ Qwen 48.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Our diagnostic motivates a shift from instance-level selection to entity-level construction (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS; Appendix~\ref{app:dals}) and MBR selection both fail to reliably beat greedy; degeneracy-gated selection (DGS) shows mixed results (Few-NERD $+0.92$~pp, SciERC $+0.71$~pp non-significant, CoNLL sign-reversal across models; Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms: it aggregates across samples rather than ranking them, recovering $+1.35$\,pp (SciERC) and $+1.32$\,pp (Few-NERD) via recall-driven entity aggregation (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}).
Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), and a simple alignment-based gating protocol selects the better method per dataset.
For practitioners, QE-based selective prediction provides an orthogonal, immediate payoff: routing low-confidence instances to human review yields $+5$--$8$\,pp at 80\% coverage without requiring multi-sample generation at inference time.

\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}
Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding on structured IE. Several conditions outside our experimental scope could restore selection headroom.
(a)~Models with poor calibration or in-context learning setups (without fine-tuning) produce more diverse outputs, widening the gap between candidates that consistency signals can exploit.
(b)~Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable make consistency signals the only viable selection mechanism; our structural signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) provide quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) even without model-internal access.
(c)~Ensemble or mixture-of-experts settings generate structurally diverse candidates by design, reducing instance degeneracy below the levels observed in our single-model sampling.
(d)~Tasks where the model exhibits systematic overconfidence (e.g., hallucination-prone generation) may benefit from consensus filtering, as disagreement among samples would carry more discriminative signal than in our well-calibrated fine-tuned regime.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Five confidence signals achieve reliable NER quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
Instance-level selection fails due to degeneracy and LP compression, but the correct self-consistency analogy for structured outputs is entity-level construction: aggregating entities across samples yields $+1.35$\,pp on SciERC and $+1.32$\,pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.05$).
Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a alignment-based gating protocol routes the appropriate method per dataset.
For practitioners: use QE-based selective prediction when deployment requires reliability guarantees; apply entity construction when multi-sample generation is feasible; assess LP-alignment via held-out validation to choose between construction and LP selection.
As models improve, degeneracy rises and the selection window narrows; content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} may be needed to close the remaining gap.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP gains are associated with strong LP-quality alignment (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two factors constrain selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) limits the available headroom, and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample) prevents exploiting the remainder.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 48.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation disentangles the two factors: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5--0.7; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Within fixed settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness: the SciERC epoch ablation shows LP gains varying with training-induced degeneracy (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}). Across 23 dataset-model-temperature configurations ($N{=}8$), however, degeneracy alone does not predict LP direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$); LP signal quality and dataset characteristics are required for cross-dataset prediction.
Temperature and training convergence are controllable levers for degeneracy (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 86.5\% vs.\ Qwen 48.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Our diagnostic motivates a shift from instance-level selection to entity-level construction (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS; Appendix~\ref{app:dals}) and MBR selection both fail to reliably beat greedy; degeneracy-gated selection (DGS) shows mixed results (Few-NERD $+0.92$~pp, SciERC $+0.71$~pp non-significant, CoNLL sign-reversal across models; Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms: it aggregates across samples rather than ranking them, recovering $+1.67$\,pp (SciERC) and $+0.88$\,pp (Few-NERD) via LP-weighted entity aggregation (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}).
Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), and a simple alignment-based gating protocol selects the better method per dataset.
For practitioners, QE-based selective prediction provides an orthogonal, immediate payoff: routing low-confidence instances to human review yields $+5$--$8$\,pp at 80\% coverage without requiring multi-sample generation at inference time.

\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}
Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding on structured IE. Several conditions outside our experimental scope could restore selection headroom.
(a)~Models with poor calibration or in-context learning setups (without fine-tuning) produce more diverse outputs, widening the gap between candidates that consistency signals can exploit.
(b)~Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable make consistency signals the only viable selection mechanism; our structural signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) provide quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) even without model-internal access.
(c)~Ensemble or mixture-of-experts settings generate structurally diverse candidates by design, reducing instance degeneracy below the levels observed in our single-model sampling.
(d)~Tasks where the model exhibits systematic overconfidence (e.g., hallucination-prone generation) may benefit from consensus filtering, as disagreement among samples would carry more discriminative signal than in our well-calibrated fine-tuned regime.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP gains are associated with strong LP-quality alignment (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two factors constrain selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) limits the available headroom, and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample) prevents exploiting the remainder.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 48.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation disentangles the two factors: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5--0.7; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Within fixed settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness: the SciERC epoch ablation shows LP gains varying with training-induced degeneracy (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}). Across 23 dataset-model-temperature configurations ($N{=}8$), however, degeneracy alone does not predict LP direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$); LP signal quality and dataset characteristics are required for cross-dataset prediction.
Temperature and training convergence are controllable levers for degeneracy (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 86.5\% vs.\ Qwen 48.4\% on CoNLL; LLaMA 23.4\% vs.\ Qwen 12.7\% on Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Our diagnostic motivates a shift from instance-level selection to entity-level construction (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS; Appendix~\ref{app:dals}) and MBR selection both fail to reliably beat greedy; degeneracy-gated selection (DGS) shows mixed results (Few-NERD $+0.92$~pp, SciERC $+0.71$~pp non-significant, CoNLL sign-reversal across models; Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms: it aggregates across samples rather than ranking them, recovering $+1.67$\,pp (SciERC) and $+0.88$\,pp (Few-NERD) via LP-weighted entity aggregation (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}).
Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), and a simple alignment-based gating protocol selects the better method per dataset.
For practitioners, QE-based selective prediction provides an orthogonal, immediate payoff: routing low-confidence instances to human review yields $+5$--$8$\,pp at 80\% coverage without requiring multi-sample generation at inference time.

\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}
Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding on structured IE. Several conditions outside our experimental scope could restore selection headroom.
(a)~Models with poor calibration or in-context learning setups (without fine-tuning) produce more diverse outputs, widening the gap between candidates that consistency signals can exploit.
(b)~Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable make consistency signals the only viable selection mechanism; our structural signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) provide quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) even without model-internal access.
(c)~Ensemble or mixture-of-experts settings generate structurally diverse candidates by design, reducing instance degeneracy below the levels observed in our single-model sampling.
(d)~Tasks where the model exhibits systematic overconfidence (e.g., hallucination-prone generation) may benefit from consensus filtering, as disagreement among samples would carry more discriminative signal than in our well-calibrated fine-tuned regime.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Five confidence signals achieve reliable NER quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
Instance-level selection fails due to degeneracy and LP compression, but the correct self-consistency analogy for structured outputs is entity-level construction: LP-weighted entity aggregation yields $+1.67$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$) and $+0.88$\,pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$).
Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a alignment-based gating protocol routes the appropriate method per dataset.
For practitioners: use QE-based selective prediction when deployment requires reliability guarantees; apply entity construction when multi-sample generation is feasible; assess LP-alignment via held-out validation to choose between construction and LP selection.
As models improve, degeneracy rises and the selection window narrows; content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} may be needed to close the remaining gap.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Two factors shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples produce identical F1, (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) limits the available headroom; (b)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to MBR utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably predict instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.38 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82, CoNLL EM). \textbf{Right}: quality estimation does not translate to selection; all methods approximately match greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (AUPRC 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
    LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (\S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as the correct self-consistency analogy.}
    Rather than selecting one of $N$ outputs, LP-weighted entity aggregation yields $+1.67$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$) and $+0.88$\,pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes all three evaluated datasets.
\end{enumerate}

20	# 论文写作质量指南（NeurIPS 实战经验）
21	
22	> 来源：2026 年 NeurIPS 投稿期间，从 20+ 项目的人工审查反馈中提炼。
23	> 每条规则都源自真实的 bug / 退回 / 审稿质疑。
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 一、数据诚信与溯源（最高优先级）
28	
29	### 1.1 数字必须有源头
30	
31	- 论文中**每一个数字**必须可追溯到 registry 实验 ID 或原始结果文件
32	- 禁止凭记忆写数字——必须 `cat result.json | head` + `ls -la` 附上文件证据
33	- 计算值（均值、标准差、DID、delta）必须独立重算，不信 Agent 第一手汇报
34	- `paper_provenance.yaml` 覆盖率必须 100%，改数字必须同步更新 provenance
35	
36	> **教训（D149 事件）**：Agent 曾伪造完整的 metrics 数据包括 p-value，事后被 Reviewer 独立 parse JSON 抓出。从此所有关键数据必须 Reviewer 独立验证到字段级别。
37	
38	### 1.2 不同来源数据不能混用
39	
40	- 配对数据必须同 seed、同 c 值、同 N、同 evaluation protocol
41	- 两张表如果 protocol 不同（如 0-shot vs 8-shot），论文必须明确说明
42	- 跨 config 比较 delta 会引入系统误差——必须补跑同 config baseline 后才能比较
43	- 非等量对比必须显式标注（如 "at unmatched volumes"）
44	
45	> **教训（D027 事件）**：不同 config 文件的 baseline 不同，跨 config 比较 delta 值引入了 artifact。
46	
47	### 1.3 结论撤回后不可复活
48	
49	- 被 Director shelved 的数据（如因截断混淆），禁止重新引入论文
50	- `paper_provenance.yaml` 中 `verified: false` 的 claim，不得恢复
51	- 术语修正后不可回退（如 "same norm" → "same per-layer standard deviation"）

55	## 二、Claim 强度与数据匹配
56	
57	### 2.1 Claim 强度规则
58	
59	| 数据支撑 | 允许的最强表述 |
60	|----------|--------------|
61	| 单 seed, 单数据集 | "preliminary observation", "initial evidence" |
62	| 单 seed, 多数据集 | "suggestive pattern", "indicative trend" |
63	| 多 seed, 单数据集 | 报告均值±标准差，可写 "we find" |
64	| 多 seed, 多数据集 | 可用 "robust", "consistent" |
65	| 统计检验显著 | 可用 "significant", 附 p-value |
66	| 单 seed + 外推到其他条件 | 必须加限定，不能声称 "scale-invariant" 等 |
67	
68	### 2.2 禁止的过强表述

70	- "remarkably stable" → 改为 "relatively stable" 或给出量化波动范围
71	- "confirmed" → 仅 "suggestive" 级别数据不能用
72	- "scale-invariant" → single-seed 验证不够
73	- "We attribute X to Y" → 如果是假说，必须改为 "We hypothesize" + "requiring causal verification"

# 论文写作质量指南（NeurIPS 实战经验）

> 来源：2026 年 NeurIPS 投稿期间，从 20+ 项目的人工审查反馈中提炼。
> 每条规则都源自真实的 bug / 退回 / 审稿质疑。

---

## 一、数据诚信与溯源（最高优先级）

### 1.1 数字必须有源头

- 论文中**每一个数字**必须可追溯到 registry 实验 ID 或原始结果文件
- 禁止凭记忆写数字——必须 `cat result.json | head` + `ls -la` 附上文件证据
- 计算值（均值、标准差、DID、delta）必须独立重算，不信 Agent 第一手汇报
- `paper_provenance.yaml` 覆盖率必须 100%，改数字必须同步更新 provenance

> **教训（D149 事件）**：Agent 曾伪造完整的 metrics 数据包括 p-value，事后被 Reviewer 独立 parse JSON 抓出。从此所有关键数据必须 Reviewer 独立验证到字段级别。

### 1.2 不同来源数据不能混用

- 配对数据必须同 seed、同 c 值、同 N、同 evaluation protocol
- 两张表如果 protocol 不同（如 0-shot vs 8-shot），论文必须明确说明
- 跨 config 比较 delta 会引入系统误差——必须补跑同 config baseline 后才能比较
- 非等量对比必须显式标注（如 "at unmatched volumes"）

> **教训（D027 事件）**：不同 config 文件的 baseline 不同，跨 config 比较 delta 值引入了 artifact。

### 1.3 结论撤回后不可复活

- 被 Director shelved 的数据（如因截断混淆），禁止重新引入论文
- `paper_provenance.yaml` 中 `verified: false` 的 claim，不得恢复
- 术语修正后不可回退（如 "same norm" → "same per-layer standard deviation"）

---

## 二、Claim 强度与数据匹配

### 2.1 Claim 强度规则

| 数据支撑 | 允许的最强表述 |
|----------|--------------|
| 单 seed, 单数据集 | "preliminary observation", "initial evidence" |
| 单 seed, 多数据集 | "suggestive pattern", "indicative trend" |
| 多 seed, 单数据集 | 报告均值±标准差，可写 "we find" |
| 多 seed, 多数据集 | 可用 "robust", "consistent" |
| 统计检验显著 | 可用 "significant", 附 p-value |
| 单 seed + 外推到其他条件 | 必须加限定，不能声称 "scale-invariant" 等 |

### 2.2 禁止的过强表述

- "remarkably stable" → 改为 "relatively stable" 或给出量化波动范围
- "confirmed" → 仅 "suggestive" 级别数据不能用
- "scale-invariant" → single-seed 验证不够
- "We attribute X to Y" → 如果是假说，必须改为 "We hypothesize" + "requiring causal verification"
- "roughly twice" → 实际比值必须在 1.8x-2.2x 才能用，否则改为更准确的近似
- "domain-agnostic" → 改为 "robust across N domains tested"

### 2.3 Claim 降级机制

当证据不足以支撑独立 claim 时，应降级为 discussion 中的定性讨论，而非删除。具体做法：
- 独立 contribution → Discussion 段落
- 硬 claim → 加 caveat 的软 claim
- 正文数字 → 移入 Appendix

---

## 三、叙事与 Storytelling

### 3.1 结构原则

- 核心 paradox/发现之间必须有**过渡句**桥接，不能让读者在关键处断线
- Introduction 每条 Contribution 必须有对应的 section/table 支撑
- Discussion 不应重复 Results 的具体数字——引用表格编号
- 同一解释不要在多处重复推导——主文写一次 + 指向 Appendix
- Limitations 段不要写成一个 17 行大段——拆分为 2-3 个子段按主题分组

### 3.2 冷引用（Cold Reference）

- 任何首次出现的概念必须有上文铺垫
- Introduction 贡献列表中不能突然出现未被提及的模型/方法名

### 3.3 不要用旧叙事套新数字

新 baseline 出来后若 delta 大幅变化，Section 的叙事逻辑必须重写，不是简单替换数字。

### 3.4 Contingency Plan

关键实验结果不确定时需预写两套叙事（如 "若结果 A → 叙事 A"、"若结果 B → 叙事 B"），实验完成后选择正确版本。提交前必须确认只留了一套。

### 3.5 不要基于中间值做叙事决策

70% 进度时的估计往往不够稳定（尤其 GSM8K 等难度分布不均匀的 benchmark），必须等完整数据再定稿叙事。

---

## 四、术语与一致性

### 4.1 术语一致性

- 全文必须统一使用正式定义的术语，不得出现同义词漂移
- 术语定义后，每次使用必须完全一致（不要有时 "perturbation sensitivity" 有时 "perturbation impact"）

### 4.2 统计量一致性

- 两个不同的 kappa/p-value 每次出现时必须标注是哪个
- 同一个 metric 在不同位置的数字必须完全一致
- 修改任何数字后必须全文 grep 确认所有引用处同步

### 4.3 p-value 格式

- 无前导零、3 位小数：`p = .003`（不是 `p = 0.003`）
- 当非劣效性 p<0.001 实际由正向效应驱动时，必须加括注说明

### 4.4 例子与定义必须一致

Taxonomy 中的定义和对应示例不能自相矛盾。如果定义说 "no new content"，示例中就不能包含新信息。

---

## 五、投稿前检查清单（Pre-Submission Checklist）

### 5.1 占位符扫描（硬门禁）

提交前必须 grep 扫描，以下模式要求**零匹配**：
```
XX.XX, PLACEHOLDER, [If , TODO, TBD, \placeholder{
```
所有条件占位段落（`[If ...]`）必须替换为最终文本。

### 5.2 编译检查

- [ ] 编译零 error
- [ ] 无 `??` 未解析引用
- [ ] 无 > 1pt 的 overfull hbox
- [ ] 正文 ≤ 9 页（NeurIPS desk reject 风险）
- [ ] 使用当年 style file（`neurips_2026.sty`）
- [ ] Review 版启用行号
- [ ] 匿名审稿版无作者姓名、无致谢

### 5.3 数据完整性

- [ ] 论文所有数字与 registry/provenance 交叉验证通过
- [ ] 计算值（均值、标准差、DID、delta）独立重算确认
- [ ] 所有 evaluation protocol 差异已在论文中说明
- [ ] 多 seed 结果报告均值和标准差
- [ ] 单 seed 数据在 Limitations 中声明

### 5.4 图表检查

- [ ] 所有 figure PDF 存在且路径匹配
- [ ] 图表不超栏宽（单栏 5.5in / 全宽 6.5in）
- [ ] 图中字体 ≥ 7pt
- [ ] 小数精度全表统一
- [ ] 最优结果加粗、次优下划线
- [ ] 表格标题（caption）自包含
- [ ] Forest plot 等可视化无 dummy 值（CI_LO=-99 等）

### 5.5 引用检查

- [ ] 引用覆盖：**直接相关方法、baseline 论文、评测 benchmark 论文、理论基础**（任一缺失说明调研不充分）
- [ ] 引用密度与目标会议近年录用论文同量级
- [ ] 引用键与 bib 条目 1:1 匹配
- [ ] 无孤儿 bib 条目
- [ ] 无幻觉引用（所有被引论文实际存在）
- [ ] 近年论文的年份/会议准确
- [ ] 审稿人要求的引用全部补齐

### 5.6 匿名化检查

- [ ] 源代码无硬编码绝对路径（`/Users/...`, `/root/...`）
- [ ] 配置文件无服务器路径
- [ ] Git history 已清理 author 信息（用 fresh repo）
- [ ] 项目管理文件不得提交（AGENTS.md, memory.md, registry.yaml, task_context/ 等）
- [ ] API Keys 通过环境变量，无泄露

### 5.7 会议 Checklist 填写（如目标会议要求）

- [ ] Claims: 摘要/Introduction 准确反映实验范围
- [ ] Limitations: 正文 Limitations 段 + Appendix 补充
- [ ] Experiments: 实验设置完整（exp_id, seed, 超参, 评估 protocol）
- [ ] Reproducibility: 数据集公开、代码可用
- [ ] Statistical Significance: 多 seed 均值+标准差、置信区间
- [ ] Compute: GPU 型号、训练时间、总 GPU-hours
- [ ] Licenses: 数据集/模型引用完整
- [ ] AI Assistants: 如实声明使用情况
- [ ] 每项认真回答（不要全写 N/A）

### 5.8 叙事完整性

- [ ] Conclusion 包含所有关键限定符（如 "under greedy decoding"）
- [ ] Abstract 与正文一致（不能一个写 "single seed" 另一个已是 "10 seeds"）
- [ ] 无 Appendix Version A/B 两套叙事残留
- [ ] 无 LaTeX 注释与正文混淆
- [ ] Contribution claim 在 Introduction 中（不在 Related Work 中）
- [ ] 所有专有名词/缩写首次出现时有定义（Abstract 内缩写也必须展开）
- [ ] Introduction 与 Method/Results 讲同一条主线（idea 变化后全文逻辑一致）

### 5.9 去 AI 风格检查

- [ ] **`grep "—" paper/*.tex` 全文清零**（解释性 em-dash 必须全删，最显著的 AI 痕迹）
- [ ] **`grep " – " paper/*.tex` 全文清零**（解释性 en-dash 必须全删）
- [ ] 无 "-ing," 分词短语结尾（如 "..., demonstrating the effectiveness of..."）
- [ ] 无连续 "Furthermore" / "Moreover" / "Additionally"（同段最多 1 个）
- [ ] 无 "It is worth noting that..." / "Notably, ..."
- [ ] 无 "delve into" / "leverage" / "utilize" / "a myriad of" / "a plethora of"
- [ ] 自然段 5-8 句是正常的，不要每 2-3 句就换段

### 5.10 模板与同类论文核对

- [ ] LaTeX 模板从目标会议官网下载（不是他人转载、不是上一年）
- [ ] `\documentclass[]{}` 选项匹配 review / camera-ready 阶段
- [ ] 写作前已参考 2-3 篇同领域近 1-2 年优秀论文，叙事节奏对齐

---

## 六、Reviewer 审查标准

### 6.1 CRITICAL 级别（必须修复才能提交）

- 论文数字与实验数据不一致
- Abstract 与正文矛盾
- Evaluation protocol 混淆（如 0-shot 写成 8-shot）
- 未经验证的数据写入论文
- 占位符残留

### 6.2 WARNING 级别（应当修复）

- Stale claims（更新了某处数字但忘了同步其他位置）
- 过强措辞不匹配数据支撑
- 隐式全因子设计误导（如写 "3×3×3=27" 但实际只有 15 格）
- 评估指标只描述了部分 domain
- 旧版数据引用

### 6.3 数据一致性审查流程

1. 从 registry 提取所有实验 metrics
2. 对照论文中每一个内联数字（到行号级别）
3. 独立重算所有衍生值
4. 不一致处标注为 CRITICAL
5. 近似表述检查实际比值是否在允许范围内

---

## 七、常见反模式速查表

| 反模式 | 症状 | 修复方式 |
|--------|------|----------|
| Stale claim | 论文某处还引用旧数字 | 改数字后全文 grep 同步 |
| Protocol 混淆 | 不同表格用了不同 evaluation 但没说明 | 每张表注明 protocol |

| 冷引用 | 首次出现的概念无铺垫 | 先建立框架再引入 |
| 定义-例子矛盾 | Taxonomy 定义和示例冲突 | 审查所有定义与其示例 |
| Placeholder 残留 | XX.XX, TODO, [If...] 未清理 | 提交前 grep 硬门禁 |
| Path 泄露 | 代码/config 含服务器绝对路径 | 改为相对路径 |
| 重复推导 | 同一解释在 3 处各自推导一遍 | 主文一次 + 引用 Appendix |
| Discussion 重复 Results | Discussion 大量复制 Results 数字 | 改为引用表格编号 |
| 单 seed overclaim | 单 seed 数据声称 scale-invariant | 加 preliminary/hedging 限定 |
| Registry 不同步 | Registry 面值与实际状态不一致 | 以 SSH 实测为准 |
| vLLM 静默失败 | max_model_len 太小导致 100% 400 错误 | 预检必须发真实 prompt 验证 |

---

## 八、写论文前加载的 Skills

写论文或做最终审查时，Director/Agent 应按需加载以下 skills：
- `latex-paper` — LaTeX 编译与格式
- `reference-audit` — 引用真实性审计
- `academic-writer` — ML 学术写作规范
- `paper-quality-lessons`（本 skill）— 实战经验教训

---

## 九、附录：投稿经验时间线教训

1. **论文数字锁定时机**：最终编译前 24h 锁定所有数字，之后只允许格式修改

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where LP-quality alignment is strong, but gains are absent elsewhere despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We diagnose two causes: instance degeneracy (13\textendash 87\%) and weak LP-quality alignment; degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations).
The correct self-consistency analogy for structured outputs is entity-level \textit{construction}: aggregating entities across samples improves F1 by $+0.88$ to $+1.67$\,pp ($p{<}0.005$) on datasets where instance-level selection fails or is marginal. Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; an alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes all three evaluated datasets.
\end{abstract}

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} rely on answer-level agreement.
Adaptive variants gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive}, input difficulty \cite{wang2025make, feng2025optimal}, or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}; \citet{chen2025twofailures} diagnose SC failure modes without proposing gating.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different gating signals because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.
\citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on fusion rather than selection.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, where degeneracy is most pronounced and is modulated by task structure and training convergence (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency for QA/summarization; our supervised signal combination baseline (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) suggests combination strategy is not the bottleneck.
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} learn per-sample scoring; reward model ensembles mitigate but do not eliminate reward hacking \cite{eisenstein2023helping}. Our LoRA-rank ablation (degeneracy 7.2\%, no selection improvement at $\rho{\approx}0.24$) suggests increasing diversity alone is insufficient within unsupervised signals.
Fine-tuning contributes to degeneracy \cite{kirk2024understanding}, and constrained structured outputs limit diversity recoverable by temperature scaling \cite{holtzman2020curious} or diverse decoding \cite{vijayakumar2018diverse}.
